title: Cap. III Rat. 14: conformity of decree and temporal execution — Achilles of foresight-election
latin: Rat. 14. Ultimo in loco argumentantur a conformitate quae est inter ipsum decretum electionis Divinae et temporalem exsecutionem ejusdem, hanc in modum; Eodem ordine quo res in tempore mandantur exsecutioni, Deus ab aeternitate decrevit ut mandarentur. Pertinet enim ad immutabilitatem voluntatis Divinae, ut non aliter agat in tempore, quam ab omni aeternitate se acturum esse decrevit. Quandoquidem igitur in temporali exsecutione salutis electorum, neminem perducit ad gloriam nisi intuitu bonorum operum et perseverantiae finalis, non potuit ab aeterno aliter ad gloriam illos eligere nisi ex eodem intuitu. Nam si ante jacta mundi fundamenta illos ad gloriam elegit gratuito, et non ex operibus praevisis, et cum ad exsecutionem ventum fuerit, non vult illis dare gloriam nisi ex operibus, mutavit voluntatem suam, quod est Divina sapientia indignissimum. Omnes Papistae qui electionem ex operibus praevisis fieri contendunt, huic argumento valde confidunt, et quasi Achilleum esse jactitant.
pass_a: Reason 14. Last in place they argue from the conformity which is between the decree of the Divine election itself and the temporal execution of the same, in this manner: In the same order in which things in time are put into execution, God from eternity decreed that they should be put. For it belongs to the immutability of the Divine will, that he not act otherwise in time than from all eternity he decreed that he would act. Since therefore in the temporal execution of the elect's salvation he leads no one to glory except in view of good works and final perseverance, he could not from eternity otherwise elect them to glory except from the same view. For if before the foundations of the world were laid he elected them to glory gratuitously, and not from foreseen works, and when it comes to execution he is unwilling to give them glory except from works, he has changed his will, which is most unworthy of the Divine wisdom. All the Papists who contend that election is made from foreseen works trust greatly in this argument, and boast that it is as it were Achilles.
pass_b: Rat. 14. Last they argue from the conformity between God's election decree and its temporal execution: in the same order in which things are executed in time, God from eternity decreed they should be executed. Divine immutability requires he not act otherwise in time than he from eternity decreed he would. So since in temporal execution he leads none of the elect to glory except in view of good works and final perseverance, he could not from eternity elect them to glory except under that same view. If before the world's foundations he elected them to glory freely, not from foreseen works, yet at execution will not give glory except from works, he has changed his will — most unworthy of divine wisdom. All Papists who hold election from foreseen works trust this argument heavily and boast it is their Achilles.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14: distinguish electing act from eternal life elected — dispositive vs motive
latin: Sol. Ut hoc argumentum recte solvatur, distinguendum est inter ipsam actionem Dei eligentis ad vitam aeternam, et ipsam rem ad quam eligit, hoc est, ipsam vitam aeternam. Potest enim habere vim causae dispositivae quoad productionem rei, quod nullam habuit vim causae motivae quoad intentionem eligentis. Non imus inficias, bona opera, sive vitam sanctam et piam, isto modo operari ad consecutionem vitae aeternae, atque Deum ab aeterno intuitum fuisse hanc electorum sanctam vitam, tanquam praecedaneam ad illorum introitum in regnum caeleste.
pass_a: Solution. That this argument may be rightly solved, a distinction must be made between the action itself of God electing to eternal life, and the thing itself to which he elects, that is, eternal life itself. For something can have the force of a dispositive cause with respect to the production of the thing, which had no force of a motive cause with respect to the intention of the one electing. We do not deny that good works, or a holy and pious life, in that manner work toward the attainment of eternal life, and that God from eternity looked upon this holy life of the elect as preceding their entrance into the heavenly kingdom.
pass_b: Sol. To solve this rightly, distinguish God's act of electing to eternal life from the thing elected — eternal life itself. What can be a dispositive cause of producing the thing need not have been a motive cause of the elector's intention. We do not deny that good works, or a holy and pious life, work that way toward attaining eternal life, and that God from eternity looked on the elect's holy life as preceding their entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

lemmas.lemma: actionem eligentis / rem ad quam eligit

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14: adversaries conflate antecedents of glory with antecedents of God's intention
latin: Sed in hoc labuntur adversarii, quod arbitrantur ea quae sunt antecedentia ad vitam aeternam, ad quam homines eliguntur, concipi etiam necessario oportere ut antecedentia ad actum sive intentionem eligentis, id est, Dei decretum, a quo eliguntur. Nam actus ille internus et aeternus voluntatis Divinae, quo eligit, et gloria, sive caeleste gaudium, ad quod eligit, sunt valde diversa. Unde possumus aliquid recte affirmare de objecto, quod non possumus nisi falso affirmare de actu sive intentione Dei qua illud objectum singulari personae destinatur. Verbi causa; Vera est haec assertio de objecto: Vocatio Pauli, justificatio, et pia vita sive operatio videntur a Deo ut praecedanea ad ejus glorificationem: sed falsa est eadem si ad actum Dei accommodetur, hoc modo, Vocatio Pauli, et justificatio, et pia vita sive operatio videntur a Deo ut praecedanea ad intentionem Divinam de Paulo glorificando.
pass_a: But in this the adversaries slip, that they think those things which are antecedents to eternal life, to which men are elected, must also necessarily be conceived as antecedents to the act or intention of the one electing, that is, to God's decree by which they are elected. For that internal and eternal act of the Divine will by which he elects, and glory, or heavenly joy, to which he elects, are greatly diverse. Whence we can rightly affirm something of the object which we cannot affirm except falsely of the act or intention of God by which that object is destined to a singular person. For example: This assertion about the object is true: Paul's calling, justification, and pious life or working are seen by God as preceding his glorification: but the same is false if it is fitted to God's act in this manner: Paul's calling, and justification, and pious life or working are seen by God as preceding the Divine intention concerning glorifying Paul.
pass_b: Here the adversaries slip: they think what precedes eternal life (to which men are elected) must also be conceived as preceding the elector's act or intention — God's decree by which they are elected. But that internal eternal act of the divine will by which he elects, and the glory or heavenly joy to which he elects, are greatly different. So we can rightly affirm of the object what we can only falsely affirm of God's act or intention destinating that object to a particular person. Example — true of the object: Paul's calling, justification, and pious life are seen by God as preceding his glorification. False if fitted to God's act: those same are seen by God as preceding the divine intention to glorify Paul.

lemmas.gloss: antecedents of life vs of intention

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14: same execution order granted — opposite order of intention denied
latin: Damus ergo, Deum eodem ordine quo in tempore mandat res exsecutioni, decrevisse ab aeterno et praevidisse quod mandarentur: sed negamus, eo ordine quo mandat exsecutioni, aut decrevit mandare, etiam intendisse. Nam cum in actibus voluntatis et mentis Divinae per se nulla sit prioritas aut posterioritas ordinis, secundum nostrum modum intelligendi, et rerum ipsarum habitudinem, non idem, sed plane oppositus ordo concipiendus est in exsecutione atque intentione Divina. Decretum exsecutionis orditur semper ab eo quod est remotius ab ipso fine, et sic gradatim progreditur ad effectionem finis: hoc sensu; Deus decrevit vocare Paulum prius quam justificare, justificare et bonis operibus ornare prius quam glorificare. Cum enim decretum exsecutionis, vel voluntas exsecutiva respiciat externam et actualem rei effectionem, illud prius ad hanc voluntatem referatur necesse est quod prius concurrit ad rem efficiendam. Jam vero e contra, Intentio voluntatis orditur semper ab ipso fine, et a fine sic ad media progreditur, ut semper prius id velit quod est fini propinquius.
pass_a: We grant therefore that God in the same order in which in time he puts things into execution decreed from eternity and foresaw that they would be put: but we deny that in the order in which he puts into execution, or decreed to put, he also intended. For since in the acts of the Divine will and mind there is of themselves no priority or posteriority of order, according to our mode of understanding and the relation of the things themselves, not the same but a plainly opposite order is to be conceived in Divine execution and intention. The decree of execution always begins from that which is more remote from the end itself, and so progresses step by step to the effecting of the end: in this sense; God decreed to call Paul before justifying, to justify and adorn with good works before glorifying. For since the decree of execution, or executive will, regards the external and actual effecting of the thing, that must be referred earlier to this will which earlier concurs to effecting the thing. But now on the contrary, the intention of the will always begins from the end itself, and from the end so progresses to the means that it always wills earlier that which is nearer the end.
pass_b: So we grant God decreed from eternity and foresaw that things would be executed in the same order he executes them in time — but we deny he also intended in that execution-order. In the acts of the divine will and mind there is of themselves no priority of order; on our way of understanding and the things' relation, execution and intention take plainly opposite orders. The decree of execution always starts from what is farther from the end and steps toward effecting it: God decreed to call Paul before justifying him, to justify and adorn with good works before glorifying. Executive will regards the external actual effecting, so what concurs earlier to producing the thing is referred earlier to that will. Intention, conversely, always starts from the end itself and moves to means so that it always wills first what is nearer the end.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14: servant-to-Gaul ship example — intention vs execution order
latin: Quia haec spinosiora sunt, ea exemplo apposito illustrabimus. Intendo servum meum in Galliam mittere: prius hoc volo quam de navi comparanda aliquid decerno: nunquam enim apud animum meum statuissem aut cogitassem naviculam illi praeparare, nisi prius decretum fuisset illum in Galliam transmittere. Jam cum ad exsecutionem ventum fuerit, volo prius nave comparere quam illum transmittere: Intelligo enim hanc transfretationem absque navi fieri nullo modo posse. Hic si quis objiciat me voluntatem mutasse, quia ab initio prius intendebam de transmissione quam de navi, nunc prius volo illum in navim imponere quam transmittere, quis non riserit hujusmodi argutias? Cum in una voluntate prius et posterius considerentur secundum internum ordinem volitionis, in altera secundum externum ordinem effectionis.
pass_a: Because these things are rather thorny, we will illustrate them by an example set beside them. I intend to send my servant into Gaul: I will this earlier than I decree anything about obtaining a ship: for I would never have established or thought in my mind to prepare a little ship for him, unless it had earlier been decreed to send him across into Gaul. Now when it has come to execution, I will earlier to appear with a ship than to send him across: for I understand that this crossing can in no way be done without a ship. Here if anyone objects that I have changed my will, because from the beginning I intended earlier concerning the sending across than concerning the ship, and now I will earlier to put him into the ship than to send him across, who would not laugh at such subtleties? Since in one will the earlier and later are considered according to the internal order of willing, in the other according to the external order of effecting.
pass_b: These points are thorny, so an example: I intend to send my servant into Gaul — I will that before I decree anything about getting a ship; I would never have thought to prepare him a little boat unless sending him to Gaul had already been decided. At execution I will to have the ship ready before sending him across, since the crossing cannot happen without a ship. If someone objects that I changed my will — because at first I intended the crossing before the ship, and now I will to put him aboard before sending him across — who would not laugh at such subtleties? In one will earlier and later follow the internal order of willing; in the other, the external order of effecting.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 14 close: Peter to heaven — same will, diverse habitude; Papist case ends
latin: Accommodemus haec instituto nostro: Deus intendit Petrum in Caelum transmittere: prius hoc vult quam media efficacia et infallibilia illi decernit: nunquam enim statuisset talia media illi suppeditare, nisi prius efficaciter decrevisset caelestem gloriam illi donare. Verum jam ad exsecutionem descendatur, Deus vult ut prius gratiae particeps fiat, ex gratia bene operetur, in bonis operibus ad finem usque perseveret, quam ad portum caelestis gloriae appellat. Hic si Jesuiticus aliquis disputator insurgat et vociferetur, Deum mutasse voluntatem suam, quia ab initio prius intendebat Petro gloriam quam gratiam aut perseverantiam in bonis operibus, nunc vult e contra ut prius gratia imbuatur, et in bonis operibus perseveranter ambulet, quam ad gloriam perveniat, ridebo hominis ineptias, et dicam diversam hanc considerationem, quoad intentionem et productionem ejusdem rei, non ponere in Deo diversam aut mutabilem voluntatem, sed ejusdem voluntatis ad eandem rem sub diversis considerationibus diversam habitudinem. Haec fere ea sunt quae a Papistis disputantur pro electione ex praevisis operibus.
pass_a: Let us accommodate these things to our purpose: God intends to send Peter across into Heaven: he wills this earlier than he decrees efficacious and infallible means for him: for he would never have established to supply such means to him, unless he had earlier efficaciously decreed to give him heavenly glory. But now let it descend to execution: God wills that he first become a partaker of grace, from grace work well, persevere in good works unto the end, before he puts in at the harbor of heavenly glory. Here if some Jesuit disputant rise up and cry out that God has changed his will, because from the beginning he intended glory for Peter earlier than grace or perseverance in good works, and now wills on the contrary that he first be imbued with grace and walk perseveringly in good works before he arrives at glory, I will laugh at the man's ineptitudes, and will say that this diverse consideration, as to intention and production of the same thing, does not posit in God a diverse or changeable will, but a diverse habitude of the same will toward the same thing under diverse considerations. These are nearly those things which are disputed by the Papists for election from foreseen works.
pass_b: Fit this to our case: God intends to send Peter into Heaven — he wills that before he decrees efficacious, infallible means for him; he would never have resolved to supply such means unless he had first efficaciously decreed to give him heavenly glory. At execution God wills that Peter first share in grace, work well from grace, and persevere in good works to the end, before he makes harbor at heavenly glory. If some Jesuit disputant rises and shouts that God changed his will — because at first he intended glory for Peter before grace or perseverance, and now wills the reverse, grace and persevering good works before glory — I will laugh at the man's folly, and say this diverse consideration of intention and production of the same thing does not posit a diverse or changeable will in God, but a diverse habitude of the same will toward the same thing under diverse considerations. That is nearly all the Papists dispute for election from foreseen works.

lemmas.gloss: diverse habitude of the same will
